feed.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion

entry.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion
entry.summary: Recent advancements in the open-source mining ecosystem have brought renewed attention to decentralized mining pool protocols, such as Sv2, DATUM, and the [Open Mining Stack](https://www.256foundation.org/). These protocols aim to address longstanding scalability and fairness issues that earlier systems like P2Pool encountered, particularly the difficulty of distributing coinbase-native payouts to large numbers of miners. The challenge centers on fixed output slots and block space limitations inherent in Bitcoin’s protocol, as well as an expanded attack surface due to the decentralized nature of these pools. Decentralized coinbase payout protocols (DCPPs) must navigate three principal design constraints. Direct coinbase payments to each miner do not scale with current output limits. Expanding the number of outputs increases vulnerability to payout settlement griefing (PSG) attacks, whereby attackers can make payouts unreliable or uncompetitive and thus threaten the economic viability of decentralized pools. Moreover, the limited scripting capabilities of Bitcoin restrict how sophisticated and fair payout mechanisms can become at the protocol level. When the number of miners seeking payment exceeds the available coinbase output slots, pools often prioritize top contributors by hashrate—a practice known as the “rich list” method. However, this exposes the system to Rich List Attacks (RLA), where miners split their hashrate across multiple identities to maximize their chances of obtaining payout slots, disadvantaging smaller miners and complicating fair distribution. As a result, robust rules and innovative technical solutions are needed to ensure equitable, eventually consistent payments. Proposed solutions have explored various models for addressing these challenges. Chris Belcher’s 2017 [payment hub proposal](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=2135429.0) introduced a central hub managing off-chain payment channels, using multisig and timelocks for security. [Braidpool’s Rolling Coinbase Aggregation](https://github.com/braidpool/braidpool/blob/8d3c5198593d691f50ae5238cdaee215f4213cda/docs/braidpool_spec.mdpayout-update) batches rewards into a single UTXO, periodically distributing payouts through multi-party signatures. P2Poolv2 proposes a [market-driven approach](https://github.com/p2poolv2/p2poolv2/wiki/Payout-mechanism---Trading-Shares-For-Bitcoin), letting miners trade sharechain UTXOs for Lightning payments, aggregating value to secure coinbase slots via market makers. Despite these innovations, vulnerabilities remain; identity splitting, control over signing authorities, and market manipulation continue to pose risks. An ideal payout protocol would allow every participant to receive a proportional, enforceable claim, freely transferable or atomically swappable, with costs shared fairly. Achieving this within Bitcoin’s existing scripting and covenant limitations remains unresolved. Practical designs must balance technical feasibility against fairness and security. Notably, tools such as Bitcoin script and external liquidity markets are essential to developing resilient architectures. Coinpool-style constructions offer a promising direction, especially when coupled with pre-signed exit transactions and threshold key management, enabling unilateral withdrawal and reducing reliance on cooperative behavior. Integrations with structures like Spark or Ark within frameworks such as P2Poolv2 illustrate practical implementations, although these too introduce new vectors for attack, such as the "poison pill" scenario where attackers inflate claims to burden market makers. The introduction of standardized terminology, including PSG and RLA, has greatly improved discourse around decentralized payout issues, allowing more precise analysis of systemic weaknesses and adversarial strategies. Historical data from P2Pool reveals both the growth and technical ceilings inherent in earlier decentralized pools. For instance, the number of addresses paid per block increased significantly from 2012 to 2014, sometimes exceeding 500 in one transaction, before hardware and software constraints imposed stricter limits. This scaling ceiling is not merely a product of adversarial action but also a natural consequence of network expansion and protocol limitations. Analyzing the experiences of P2Pool highlights the impact of share difficulty adjustments and dust thresholds on small miners. When payouts per block fell below certain levels, miners were effectively excluded, not by targeted attack but by organic scaling pressure. A comprehensive CSV dataset detailing P2Pool coinbase payouts is available for further study at [https://www.learnbitcoin.com/downloads/p2pool-coinbases.csv](https://www.learnbitcoin.com/downloads/p2pool-coinbases.csv). Various actors, including established pools and large miners, may attempt to undermine decentralized payout systems through subtle forms of griefing. By redirecting hash power or fragmenting it across multiple identities, they can degrade the competitiveness of decentralized pools without incurring significant personal cost, making such strategies both effective and difficult to detect. Block withholding and payout griefing represent potent threats, emphasizing the need for payout mechanisms that strictly tie selection probability to total value, regardless of identity partitioning.
